newsitem.title: USA: Recessions may just be good for your health -- study.
newsitem.headline: Recessions may just be good for your health -- study.

text.p: As the economy enters another year of expansion and low unemployment, new research suggests that loss of a job may actually contribute to a healthier, longer life for at least some Americans.

Christopher Ruhm, a professor of economics at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, has concluded in a study that higher unemployment may lead to lower overall mortality rates and reduce fatalities from several major causes of death.

The provocative findings, published recently by the National Bureau of Economic Research, run counter to earlier studies showing higher unemployment rates lead to more stress and riskier behaviour, causing both mental and physical health to deteriorate over time.
The new research suggests that employment itself may have an adverse impact on health, with job-related stress and hazardous working conditions both taking their toll.
Joblessness, for example, may give individuals more time to exercise, to prepare more healthful meals or to schedule medical appointments for themselves or their dependents.

Those who lose lower-income jobs, which often lack employer-provided health insurance, may also become eligible for federally funded Medicaid, which would lower their health-care costs, the study's author noted.
The new study, which looks at state-level data compiled between 1972 and 1991, suggests that a one percentage point rise in the unemployment rate lowers the total death rate by 0.5 percent.
Ruhm also found that a one percentage point increase in unemployment has the biggest impact on younger individuals, lowering the death rate for those aged between 20 and 44 by 1.3 percent.

A similar increase in joblessness is also linked to reduced deaths from car accidents, other accidents, homicide and liver ailments by 2.4 percent, 1.7 percent, 1.5 percent and 0.8 percent, respectively.
Death rates from cancer, heart disease and other major causes of death also fell but by smaller margins.
Suicide, however, proved to be an exception to the overall findings. Suicide rates increased by 0.7 percent for each percentage rise in unemployment.
Economists who follow the job market found the new research intriguing but said they were unswayed by the findings.

"The blunt fact is I think most people are happier when they're employed than unemployed," said David Wyss, a research director at DRI/McGraw-Hill. "The research seems right. My basic problem is I don't really believe it."

Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd., added, "The conclusions of the study seem somewhat bothersome, given the premium that is placed in our society on holding a job. If you're unemployed, rather than creating less stress and pressures, it tends to create more."
One psychologist offered this reaction to the findings:
"I think it's important to start getting the news out that recessions are adaptive challenges," said George Greenberg, a psychologist on the clinical faculty of Cornell Medical Centre in New York.
But he added, "It would be hard to prove that recessions are good -- except that they are challenges to people."
In any case, the study is likely to cause a stir in economic circles.
"It will undoubtedly spawn an enormous amount of research," predicted Uwe Reinhardt, professor of economics and public affairs at Princeton University.
"It's a fantastic intellectual curiousity, (but) it begs for absolutely no policy intervention."
